segs.text: Section twenty. Idiosyncratic and immunologic responses. These two toxic endpoints fit neither the organ-specific nor the non-organ-specific group. The slide defines an idiosyncratic reaction as genetically determined abnormal reactivity to a chemical. The response is qualitatively similar to other people's, but extreme. Using the word idiosyncratic for every low-frequency reaction is not proper use of the term.

She said, the liver is the organ that is most likely to have an idiosyncratic reaction compared to other organs in the body. The reason is that the liver does most drug metabolism. A person with a rare genetic variant may metabolize a drug differently and form a toxic metabolite that others do not. Before pharmacogenomics this looked unexplainable. With the genotype known, it is an unusual but explained reaction.

The next slide is titled Allergic Responses. She asked the class to change it to immunologic responses, because allergy is only one of two kinds. In an immunologic reaction, the drug is recognized as foreign and the immune system responds to it. Small molecules, under six hundred daltons, bind body proteins and act as haptens, and the drug and protein complex triggers the response. Large drugs, the therapeutic peptides and proteins, activate the immune system directly. So small drugs can provoke an immune response too.

The two mechanisms are hypersensitivity, meaning type one, two, three or four allergic responses, and autoimmune reactions, where the immune system attacks the patient's own body. Autoimmune reactions are increasing as more biologicals reach the market. She said, oftentimes, those immune responses to those biological therapies are hard to predict, and they're often kind of bad. An immunologic reaction can also appear in one organ. Her father's P P I reaction appeared as interstitial nephritis.

Four polls close the Toxic Responses deck. In the first, two statements are true. A delayed response may be seen weeks to years after exposure. And immediate effects can occur with each dose in a chronic exposure, such as a workplace leak that causes a headache every day. Three statements are false. Tissue injury is not always reversible, toxins can cause local effects, and a systemic effect always requires absorption into the blood. In the second poll, teratogenicity is the non-organ-specific response, because the other options each name an organ. The third and fourth polls are the liver questions from sections seventeen and eighteen.
